reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy / Braunwald's Heart Disease
clinicalPearls: An uncommon cause of exertional leg ischaemia in young, often athletic patients caused by an abnormal relationship between the popliteal artery and the surrounding musculotendinous structures
Presents with positional or exertional calf claudication, sometimes with foot paraesthesiae or coolness, in the absence of atherosclerotic risk factors
Symptoms are typically reproduced by exercise or by active plantarflexion and passive dorsiflexion, which tighten the compressing muscle
May be anatomical, from an aberrant course of the artery or medial head of gastrocnemius, or functional, from muscular hypertrophy compressing a normally positioned artery
Often bilateral, so the contralateral limb should be assessed even when only one side is symptomatic
Dynamic imaging with provocative positioning (duplex ultrasound, CT or MR angiography) is key, as resting studies can appear normal
Untreated compression can lead to arterial wall damage, aneurysm, thrombosis, or distal embolisation, so surgical release of the entrapment is the definitive treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome results from an abnormal anatomical or functional relationship between the popliteal artery and the muscles and tendons of the popliteal fossa, most often involving the medial head of gastrocnemius. In anatomical variants the artery follows an aberrant medial course or is crossed by an anomalous muscle slip, while in the functional form a normally positioned artery is compressed by hypertrophied musculature during contraction. Repeated dynamic compression, particularly during the plantarflexion of exercise, intermittently restricts arterial flow and produces exertional ischaemia. Over time the recurrent mechanical trauma damages the arterial wall, promoting intimal injury, post-stenotic dilatation or aneurysm formation, mural thrombus, and the risk of thrombotic occlusion or distal embolisation, so a functional problem can progress to fixed arterial disease.
additionalDifferentials: Cystic adventitial disease of the popliteal artery
Medial tibial stress syndrome or musculoskeletal leg pain
Deep vein thrombosis or venous claudication
additionalInvestigations: Duplex ultrasound with provocative plantarflexion and dorsiflexion manoeuvres
CT or MR angiography with dynamic positioning to demonstrate compression and define anatomy
Ankle-brachial pressure index at rest and after exercise or with positional stress
MRI of the popliteal fossa to characterise the musculotendinous anatomy
Catheter angiography with stress positioning in selected cases
Assessment of the contralateral limb given frequent bilaterality
redFlags: Acute limb ischaemia from popliteal thrombosis or distal embolisation
A popliteal aneurysm complicating chronic entrapment
Rest pain or tissue loss indicating critical ischaemia
Rapidly progressive symptoms or loss of distal pulses
reference.prognosis: When recognised before fixed arterial damage develops, surgical release of the entrapment relieves symptoms and preserves the artery with good long-term outcomes. Delayed diagnosis allowing arterial degeneration, aneurysm, or thrombosis worsens the prognosis and may require arterial reconstruction.
pitfalls: Relying on resting imaging that appears normal and omitting provocative dynamic studies
Attributing exertional leg pain to a musculoskeletal or compartment cause in a young athlete
Assessing only the symptomatic limb and missing bilateral disease
Delaying treatment until irreversible arterial damage or thrombosis has occurred
Confusing the syndrome with cystic adventitial disease, which requires different management
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
management: Surgical release of the entrapment by myotomy or division of the anomalous medial head of gastrocnemius or accessory muscle slip, which is the definitive treatment
Arterial reconstruction with bypass or interposition graft when the vessel is already damaged by stenosis, post-stenotic aneurysm or thrombosis
Activity and exercise modification to limit provocative plantarflexion while awaiting surgery
Catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy for acute thrombotic occlusion, with antiplatelet therapy to reduce embolic risk
Assessment and treatment of the contralateral limb given the frequent bilaterality
Referral to vascular surgery for early decompression before fixed arterial degeneration develops
